task: A2, the corpus collector for plan W10 stage A: seventeen open documents no run in the record has read, with a manifest, a fetcher that keeps no text in the repository, a coverage map in the skill's words, and the split frozen at eight for the arms and four in reserve.
files_written: /home/user/ThreadSmith/Workflow/rigs/W10 harness/corpus/sources.json - the manifest: 17 entries, each with the address, the trim (start/end markers, caps), the licence or open standing with how I know it, the domain, the passage that answers "why" quoted from the document, whether two named speakers or agents can be exchanged and which names, the eleven-test row, the split allocation, and a hash block (sha256 of the trimmed normalised text, sha256 of the downloaded bytes, words, chars, fetch date, what was hashed, which extractor).

/home/user/ThreadSmith/Workflow/rigs/W10 harness/corpus/fetch.py - the fetcher, modelled on the plan 49 rig's fetch.py: same trim rule and method names, plus a hard refusal to write anywhere inside the repository, hash verification on every fetch (--check, --strict), --dry-run that sends nothing, --probe and --grep/--grep-raw (how the trim markers and the why-passages were found), --write-hashes that never overwrites a frozen hash, and --audit that re-fetches and checks the manifest against the text.

/home/user/ThreadSmith/Workflow/rigs/W10 harness/corpus/split.json - the frozen split: eight for the arms, four in reserve, five held out; the rule that chose them, what the choice gives up, and which counts of plan W10 the split makes runnable.

/home/user/ThreadSmith/Workflow/rigs/W10 harness/corpus/coverage.md - the coverage map in the skill's own words: what the harness does with the corpus, the eleven tests document by document and the other way round, the six kinds of question, the eight domains, the re-identification table with occurrence counts, how I know each claim, the gaps, what the corpus cannot do, how the documents were found, and the traps.
what_it_does:
Supplies stage C with documents and the means to get them without keeping any text in the repository.

Seventeen documents, 58,290 words trimmed, each between 1,543 and 6,000 words, across all eight domains of HV file 50 (science 2, computability 2, economics 2, philosophy 2, fiction 3, design 2, rules 2, instructions 2). Every one was fetched once by the program in this folder, verified to be the document named, and hashed; the text is kept nowhere here. Nine have two named speakers or agents whose exchange changes what the document attributes to whom.

How it maps to W8's parts. Arm (x) and prediction PA.3 rest on W8 part A10, whose admitted edits at the grain of text are displacement, occlusion and re-identification: the manifest's `exchange` field gives the re-identification edit its ports (the names) and says, per document, what the exchange changes about attribution, and `--audit` reports how many times each name actually occurs, which is the size of the edit. The split puts all eight exchangeable-first documents in the arms so that the plan's frozen count, "at least four of eight documents", has a denominator of eight. Arms (a) to (f) and (r) take the same eight, three repeats per box, n = 8 as W3's P4.1 to P4.6 fix it. The four in reserve are for W3 section 8's repeat under a new sorting and carry the two domains the arms leave out. The five held out are not spent, in the way HV file 50's 33 held-out sources are not spent.

The fetcher is the interface A1's harness uses: `python3 fetch.py --out <dir outside the repository> --no-header --strict`. --strict stops a run on any document whose text no longer hashes to what was frozen today, rather than letting a changed document enter quietly.
dry_run:
Everything was run with python3 in this folder. No API was called, no key was read, nothing was sent anywhere but HTTP GETs to the public addresses in the manifest.

1. `python3 fetch.py --dry-run` - prints all 17 addresses and the frozen word counts, fetches nothing. Output ends "17 sources. Nothing was fetched and nothing was sent."
2. `python3 fetch.py --check` (all 17) - fetched every document a second time after freezing: 17/17 "in band", 17/17 "match" on the frozen text hash, "nothing was written; no text is kept in the repository". This is the test that the hash mechanism works: a second fetch reproduces the frozen text exactly.
3. `python3 fetch.py --audit` (all 17) - re-fetches and checks the manifest against the text. First run found four real faults: the why-passage quotations for W9, W13 and W15 were not in the text (I had transcribed curly apostrophes as straight ones, and dropped a space in "Relatively , to her"), W9's exchangeable name likewise, and W4's second name occurred once. I fixed the three quotations, changed W4's pair from Fermat/Poincaré (4 and 1 occurrences) to Fermat/Bernoulli (4 and 3), and re-ran: all 17 OK, with occurrence counts printed (W7 103/103 down to W13 2/2).
4. Repository guard: `python3 fetch.py --out "<...>/corpus/text" W12` exits 1 with "refusing to write inside the repository ... (the corpus text is never kept here)".
5. Writing outside: `python3 fetch.py --out <scratchpad>/w10corpus --strict W9 W12` wrote W9.txt and W12.txt with the provenance header, `--no-header` wrote W12.txt without it; both checked by head, then the directory was deleted.
6. Hash-mismatch refusal: copied sources.json to the scratchpad, set W12's text hash to 64 zeros, ran `--sources <copy> --out <dir> --strict W12 W9`: W12 "REFUSED: raw match, text DIFFERS" and no W12.txt written; W9 written. Copy and output deleted.
7. `python3 -c "import ast; ast.parse(...)"` after each in-place edit of fetch.py; a final validator script over sources.json and split.json (ids unique, every required field present and non-empty, every word count inside 1,500-6,000, every hash 64 hex characters, the three split lists in sources.json identical to split.json's, no address or title shared with the plan 49 corpus).
predictions_bearing: W10.2 (stage A): at least twelve documents with fetcher entries and at least six exchangeable. Delivered: seventeen, nine exchangeable. Falsified by fewer; it is not falsified.

Arm (x) / PA.3, from W8 part A10 (one of the two runnable predictions the owner names first): 'the emission moves on at least one certified field on at least four of eight documents'. All eight arms documents admit the name exchange, so the denominator is eight, and the manifest names the two names per document and what the exchange changes.
W10.1 (stage A): the harness dry-runs every arm on one document sending nothing. This folder supplies the documents and a fetcher whose --dry-run sends nothing; A1's harness owns the arms.
W3 P4.1 to P4.6 (stage C and D): n = 8 documents, three repeats per box, k = the (a)-to-(a) baseline plus three, tolerance two documents. The split fixes n = 8 and names the eight.
W3 section 8's repeat under a new sorting: the four in reserve, chosen to carry the two domains (economics, instructions) the arms eight leave out.

P4.7 and W8 A10's second test: *look inside* has purchase on exactly one document (W3, in the reserve) and a little on W1. coverage.md names this as the test that will be left with nothing to reach on most documents, which is what file 33 tells the reader to say and what HV file 54 already records.
W10 section 2's rule that the 33 held-out sources of HV file 50 are not spent: none of the seventeen is any of them, and five more are held out of this split.

claims.claim: No run in the record has read any of these seventeen documents.
claims.evidence: Checked document by document against the plan 49 rig's sources.json (49 entries; a program compared every address and title: 'addresses or titles shared with the plan 49 corpus: none'), against HV file 50 (the same 49 with their trims), and against HV file 43, which contains twenty-five passages written by Claude and no outside documents at all. A repository-wide search for the seventeen titles and authors found hits only in this folder's own files, plus the bare names 'Hilbert' (in DeepSeek returns on C1, C2, C3) and 'Michelson' (one return on F5), which are names inside replies, not documents read.
claims.would_count_against: any address or document of mine turning up in the plan 49 rig's sources.json, corpus folder, runs folder or in HV files 50 or 43; or a record elsewhere in the repository of a run handed one of these texts.

claims.claim: Every one of the seventeen is between 1,500 and 6,000 words after the trim, and a second fetch reproduces the same text.
claims.evidence: fetch.py --check over all 17 after the hashes were frozen: every row 'in band' and 'match'; the validator asserts 1,500 <= words <= 6,000 from the frozen hash blocks (minimum 1,543 for W15, maximum 6,000 for W7).
claims.would_count_against: a later --check printing DIFFERS or OUT OF BAND for any id; that is exactly what the hash is for, and --strict then refuses to write that document.

claims.claim: Each of the seventeen contains a passage that explains why something happened, works or should be done, and the manifest quotes that passage from the document itself.
claims.evidence: fetch.py --audit fetches each document and checks that the why_passage quotation occurs in the trimmed text with whitespace normalised; after three transcription fixes all 17 report OK. The quotations were taken from the fetcher's own --grep and --probe output, not from memory.
claims.would_count_against: a later --audit reporting 'the why_passage quotation is NOT in the text'; or a reader judging that a quoted passage states a purpose rather than a reason. W15's is the weakest on that second count and is held out of the split.

claims.claim: Nine documents have two named agents whose exchange changes what the document attributes to whom, and all eight arms documents are among them.
claims.evidence: The manifest's exchange field per document, with the counts fetch.py --audit measured in the text: W7 SOCRATES 103 / EUTHYPHRO 103, W9 Elephant's Child 38 / Crocodile 26, W10 Leopard 26 / Ethiopian 24, W17 Dr. Heidegger 25 / widow Wycherly 7, W8 CLEANTHES 22 / PHILO 9, W12 MIT 13 / New Jersey 11, W1 Fresnel 4 / Stokes 2, W4 Fermat 4 / Bernoulli 3, W13 Cardozo 2 / Andrews 2.
claims.would_count_against: a judge holding that MIT and New Jersey are places and not agents (W12), which would drop the arms to seven exchangeable; or holding that an exchange touching four tokens (W1, W4) or four (W13) is too small a change to the world to count. coverage.md says both out loud and says the judgment must be made before stage C, not after a count.

claims.claim: Nothing in this folder keeps any fetched text, and nothing can write text into the repository.
claims.evidence: fetch.py's guard() refuses any --out path under the repository root and exits 1; demonstrated on '<repo>/corpus/text'. The default mode writes nothing at all; the fetched bytes go to a tempfile.mkdtemp outside the repository and are removed in a finally block. The folder after all runs holds four files: sources.json, fetch.py, split.json, coverage.md.
claims.would_count_against: a .txt, .bin, raw/ or corpus/ directory appearing under corpus/ after a run; a find over the W10 harness folder for such files showed only A1's fixtures and prompts, none of mine.

claims.claim: Every document is openly fetchable, and where the standing is an open page rather than an open licence the manifest says which.
claims.evidence: Licences seen in the fetched text: W1 'This work is in the public domain in the United States because it was published before January 1, 1931.'; W11 'Copyright (c) 2020 IETF Trust ...' under BCP 78; W14 'License / Creative Commons - CC BY 3.0'; W15 'This document has been placed in the public domain.' Claimed with address and date: W2 the PLOS Medicine article page's CC-BY sentence; W5 that the FEE page carries no copyright or reprint line; W13 that Wikisource tags the same case PD-EdictGov; W3 ACM copyright served from a university course page; W12 the author's own site; W19 the Nobel Foundation's own site; W16 GPL-2.0 as part of the kernel tree; W4, W7, W8, W9, W10, W17 public domain by date or by Project Gutenberg's boilerplate, which the fetcher strips.

claims.claim: The eight for the arms were chosen by one stated rule, fixed before any run: every corpus document that admits the name exchange.
claims.evidence: split.json's the_rule_used_to_choose, and the fact that the eight are exactly the nine exchangeable documents minus W10, which is held for the reserve's repeat so that the same kind can be run twice without reusing a document.
claims.would_count_against: a reviewer showing that a different eight would serve the other arms better, which is the trade the rule makes: domain spread was given up for the arm (x) denominator, and economics and instructions do not reach arms (a) to (f) or (r) this round.

claims.claim: The corpus has no claim-and-critique pair, which is the one thing HV file 50 says a single document cannot supply.
claims.evidence: I looked for one, the published critique of W2, at two addresses (PubMed Central id 1855693 and the PLoS Medicine page for 10.1371/journal.pmed.0040168); the fetcher returned 528 and 695 words, both under the band, so it was dropped. No other pair was tried.
claims.would_count_against: someone finding a claim and its published critique, both between 1,500 and 6,000 words, both openly fetchable, neither in the record. 'I did not find one' describes my search and not the world.

claims.claim: Check the patches has no purchase on any of the eight arms documents.
claims.evidence: The eleven-test table in coverage.md: the five documents that carry a history of being caught out and rescued (W2, W11, W14, W16, W19) are all in the reserve or held out.
claims.would_count_against: a reader finding, in W13 or W8 or W1, a narrowing or a rescue I did not see; my reading was of quoted passages, not of whole documents.

claims.claim: The hash check can tell a cosmetic change at the server from a change to the document.
claims.evidence: Two hashes are kept: of the downloaded bytes and of the trimmed normalised text. In the deliberate-mismatch test the verdict printed was 'raw match, text DIFFERS', which names the case where the bytes are unchanged and the extraction or trim has moved.

could_not_settle:
Five things.

1. Whether an exchange of four tokens (W1, W4) or of two author lines (W13) is a large enough change to the world for arm (x) to bear on W8 part A10. The counts are reported rather than judged, because judging them after the run would be moving the goalposts. It should be settled by A5 or A4 before stage C.

2. Whether "MIT" and "New Jersey" are two named agents. They are two named design schools with named partisans in the text; if a judge says places are not agents, the arms hold seven exchangeable, not eight.

3. Whether the corpus is fitted to the arms. Every document is someone else's, written for its own purpose, and the passages quoted are the documents' own words at addresses anyone can refetch; but which seventeen were fetched, and which passage was called the "why" passage, was decided here. A corpus picked to suit an arm would flatter it, and nothing in this folder can rule that out. The only guard is that the eight were chosen by one stated rule, fixed before any run.

4. What a reader does with a long document. The 1,500-to-6,000-word band comes from the task, not from anything about explanation; it keeps out most claim-and-critique pairs and most long technical arguments.

5. Whether the licences of W3 and W12 are open enough. Both are open-access pages under someone's copyright, which the task permits ("an open-access page"), but neither is an open licence. If the owner reads it more strictly, W12 leaves the arms and the split must be redrawn.
for_the_reviewer:
Press first on the split, because it is the one place where I chose against the plan's grain.

The plan fixes arm (x) at "four of eight documents", so I made every one of the eight admit the name exchange, and paid for it with domain spread: two philosophy, two fiction, and no economics or instructions in the arms. If you think arms (a) to (f) and (r) need all eight domains more than arm (x) needs a denominator of eight, the split changes and split.json should be rewritten before stage C, not after a count.

Second, press on the three thin exchanges (W1 4/2, W4 4/3, W13 2/2). If arm (x) moves nothing on those three and moves on the other five, the count is 5 of 8 and the prediction passes, but the reading would be about the size of the edit, not about A10. Deciding now what counts as a movement on a thin document is cheaper than deciding it after.

Third, check my licence calls, especially W3 (ACM copyright, university course page) and W12 (the author's own site, in the arms). I read "openly fetchable (public domain, open licence, or an open-access page)" as covering them; a stricter reading costs W12 and the split.

Fourth, run `python3 fetch.py --audit` yourself. It found four faults in my own manifest, including two mis-transcribed quotations, and it is the cheapest check that the manifest still describes the documents. Then run `--check` on a later day: that is the test the hashes exist for.

Fifth, the gap I could not close: no pair. Five of file 50's sources were pairs, and *build the best rival*, *check the patches* and *testing against cases* lean on them. W13 (a rule and its dissent in one document) and W8 (an argument and its attacker) stand in, but an author who writes both sides chooses how strong to make the weaker one.
